1.pericope_label: Make thee bonds and yokes, and put them upon thy neck
debates: Whether the name in the heading is a transcriptional error
Why a sign is used rather than a spoken warning
What brought the foreign ambassadors to Jerusalem
outliers: Calvin defends the received heading by holding the prophecy concealed for years, a solution the others decline
themes: A date that contradicts the narrative three verses later
A prophet made to wear what he predicts
Confederacy formed out of separate defeats
Foreign empire described as part of God’s order

4.pericope_label: I have made the earth, and give it to whom it seemeth meet
debates: Whether the verb about giving the earth is past or future
Why the message is sent by the ambassadors themselves
Why the beasts of the field are included in the grant
outliers: Calvin would render the giving of the earth as future where the received version and most others make it past
themes: Creation urged as the title to dispose of kingdoms
A sign held dead unless doctrine gives it life
Confidence in allies dismantled before the threat is stated
Instinct in animals shaming the obstinacy of men

7.pericope_label: All nations shall serve him, and his son, and his son’s son
debates: How many successors the phrase son and son’s son allows
Whether the clause warns the nations or the king
Why a threat is added to a decree already announced
outliers: Ellicott notes that the whole verse is absent from the Greek, perhaps because the translators found the succession historically awkward
themes: A dynasty given a term at the moment it is granted
Kingdoms held to have fixed limits like individual lives
Threat added because warning alone had not been received
An argument from the lesser nations to the greater guilt

9.pericope_label: Hearken not to your prophets, nor to your diviners
debates: Whether the warning against diviners is addressed to the nations or to the Jews
What the five names for diviners severally mean
Why submission is promised a milder outcome than resistance
outliers: Ellicott suggests each of the five names was characteristic of one of the five nations addressed
themes: A catalogue of ways of guessing at the future
Uncertainty about the future as the appetite such men feed
Conquest ordinarily content with tribute
One verb carrying both service and cultivation

12.pericope_label: Bring your necks under the yoke of the king of Babylon, and live
debates: Why the king is addressed in the plural
Whether submission to a conqueror can be counselled as wisdom
What the prophetic office implies about a prophet’s standing before a king
outliers: Henry turns the counsel of submission into an argument for accepting a different yoke altogether
themes: A national message narrowed to one nation
Surrender urged as the way to preserve life
Warning added because kindness had not moved them
Deceivers perishing with those they deceive

15.pericope_label: They prophesy a lie in my name
debates: What distinguishes a true prophet from a false one
Whether the temple vessels were ever partly restored before the exile ended
Why the king was addressed before the priests and people
outliers: Ellicott records an apocryphal tradition of an early restoration of the vessels and judges it unhistorical
themes: A lie made worse by the name attached to it
Willing credulity treated as a chosen blindness
Priests failing at the discrimination their office required
A prediction on which the rival prophets staked their credit

17.pericope_label: If they be prophets, let them make intercession
debates: What the verb rendered make intercession properly means
Whether the list of temple furniture is original to the Hebrew text
Why the same counsel is repeated at such length
outliers: Ellicott notes that the specific inventory is missing from the Greek, which some critics take as evidence of a later addition
themes: Prolixity forced on a speaker by opposition
A prediction used as an incentive to rebellion
Rival prophets invited to pray rather than predict
Teaching and intercession treated as one office

20.pericope_label: They shall be carried to Babylon until the day that I visit them
debates: Whether the pronoun in the closing promise refers to the vessels or to the people
Whether the particle opening the twenty-first verse is affirmative or causal
Why the vessels were left when the king and nobles were taken
outliers: Calvin refers the promised visitation to the people rather than the vessels, since the restoration of the one depended on the other
themes: Restraint on a conqueror read as an unnoticed mercy
Repetition used to penetrate obduracy
A promise deliberately left without a date
Vessels valued for the sake of the people, not the reverse
